name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q01 - Activation energy and enthalpy change from potential energy diagram

questiontext.text:
The potential energy diagram for a single-step reaction \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}\) along the reaction coordinate is shown below:

Based on the given potential energy diagram, what are the values of the activation energy for the forward reaction (\(E_{a,\text{fwd}}\)) and the enthalpy change of the reaction (\(\Delta H\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Interpretation of the Diagram
From the potential energy diagram:
Potential energy of reactants \(E_{\text{reactants}} = 40\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Potential energy of the activated complex at the peak \(E_{\text{complex}} = 100\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Potential energy of products \(E_{\text{products}} = 15\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
The activation energy for the forward reaction is defined as the minimum excess energy required by reactants to reach the activated state:
\(E_{a,\text{fwd}} = E_{\text{complex}} - E_{\text{reactants}}\)
The enthalpy change of the reaction (\(\Delta H\)) is the difference between the potential energy of products and reactants:
\(\Delta H = E_{\text{products}} - E_{\text{reactants}}\)

Step 3: Calculation of Forward Activation Energy
Substitute the read values into the activation energy formula:
\(E_{a,\text{fwd}} = 100\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} - 40\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 60\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 4: Calculation of Enthalpy Change
Substitute the read values into the enthalpy change formula:
\(\Delta H = 15\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} - 40\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = -25\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
The negative sign indicates that the forward reaction is exothermic.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The activation energy for the forward reaction is \(60\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and the enthalpy change of the reaction is \(-25\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: \(E_{a,\text{fwd}} = 60\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta H = -25\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q02 - Temperature dependence of Maxwell Boltzmann kinetic energy distribution

questiontext.text:
The Maxwell–Boltzmann kinetic energy distribution curves for a gaseous reaction mixture at two temperatures \(T\) and \((T + 10)\text{ K}\) are illustrated below:

Which of the following statements correctly describes the molecular and graphical changes that occur when the temperature is raised from \(T\) to \((T + 10)\text{ K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Energy Distribution
The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution describes the spread of molecular kinetic energies in a gas. The peak of each curve corresponds to the most probable kinetic energy, which is the kinetic energy possessed by the greatest fraction of molecules.

Step 2: Effect of Temperature Elevation on Curve Shape
As temperature increases by \(10\text{ K}\) from \(T\) to \((T + 10)\text{ K}\), the thermal motion of the particles intensifies. The maximum of the curve shifts to a higher kinetic energy value along the horizontal axis, and the peak height decreases because the curve broadens out to the right.

Step 3: Conservation of Total Probability
Because the total number of molecules remains constant, the total area under each distribution curve must equal unity at all temperatures. A broader curve inevitably has a lower peak height.

Step 4: Fraction of Reactive Molecules
The shaded region beyond the activation energy threshold (\(E_a\)) represents the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy (\(E \ge E_a\)) to react. As shown in the diagram, when temperature rises by \(10\text{ K}\), the area beyond \(E_a\) roughly doubles, explaining why the reaction rate nearly doubles.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Raising the temperature causes the most probable kinetic energy to increase, the maximum peak height to decrease as the curve broadens, and the fraction of molecules having energy greater than or equal to \(E_a\) to roughly double.
Final Answer: The most probable kinetic energy increases, the peak height decreases as the distribution broadens, and the area representing molecules with \(E \ge E_a\) roughly doubles.

answer.text: The most probable kinetic energy decreases, the peak height increases, and the total area under the distribution curve increases.
The most probable kinetic energy increases, the peak height decreases as the distribution broadens, and the area representing molecules with \(E \ge E_a\) roughly doubles.
The most probable kinetic energy remains unchanged, but the value of the activation energy \(E_a\) decreases by half.
Both the most probable kinetic energy and the peak height increase because the total area under the curve increases with temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q03 - Determination of reaction order and rate constant from logarithmic plot

questiontext.text:
For the decomposition reaction of a reactant \(\mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\), a plot of natural logarithm of reactant concentration, \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\), against time \(t\) (in seconds) produces the straight line shown below:

From the linearity of this plot and the data points indicated, identify the order of the reaction and compute the value of the rate constant \(k\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph displays \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) on the vertical axis against time \(t\) (in seconds) on the horizontal axis.
Two points on the straight line are given:
At \(t_1 = 0\text{ s}\), \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]_0 = -1.609\)
At \(t_2 = 100\text{ s}\), \(\ln[\mathrm{R}] = -2.302\)

Step 2: Identification of Reaction Order
The integrated rate law for a first-order reaction is:
\(\ln[\mathrm{R}] = -kt + \ln[\mathrm{R}]_0\)
This matches the linear equation \(y = mx + c\), where a plot of \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) versus \(t\) gives a straight line with slope \(m = -k\) and vertical intercept \(c = \ln[\mathrm{R}]_0\). Since \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) versus \(t\) is linear, the reaction is of first order.

Step 3: Relevant Formula for Rate Constant
The slope of the line is defined by:
\(\text{Slope} = \frac{\ln[\mathrm{R}]_2 - \ln[\mathrm{R}]_1}{t_2 - t_1} = -k\)
Therefore, the rate constant is:
\(k = -\text{Slope} = -\frac{\ln[\mathrm{R}]_2 - \ln[\mathrm{R}]_1}{t_2 - t_1}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the coordinates of the two points:
\(k = -\frac{-2.302 - (-1.609)}{100\text{ s} - 0\text{ s}} = -\frac{-0.693}{100\text{ s}} = 0.00693\text{ s}^{-1} = 6.93 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}\)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units for a first-order rate constant are \(\text{s}^{-1}\), which correctly matches the calculated value. The reaction order is first order and the rate constant is \(6.93 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: First order with \(k = 6.93 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q04 - Catalyzed and uncatalyzed reaction energy profile analysis

questiontext.text:
The energy profiles for an uncatalyzed reaction path (solid curve) and a catalyzed reaction path (dashed curve) along the reaction coordinate are shown in the figure below:

Based on the quantitative energy values provided in the diagram, what is the activation energy for the reverse reaction in the presence of the catalyst (\(E_{a,\text{rev(cat)}}\)) and what is the enthalpy change (\(\Delta H\)) for the catalyzed reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the energy profile:
Potential energy of reactants \(= 50\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Potential energy of products \(= 20\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Potential energy peak for uncatalyzed pathway \(= 130\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Potential energy peak for catalyzed pathway \(= 90\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Principles Governing Catalyst Action
A catalyst provides an alternate pathway with a lower potential energy barrier. It lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions by the exact same amount. A catalyst does not alter the energy of reactants or products, and consequently leaves the standard enthalpy change of reaction (\(\Delta H\)) and the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Step 3: Calculation of Reverse Catalyzed Activation Energy
The activation energy for the reverse reaction in the catalyzed pathway is the energy difference between the catalyzed activated complex peak and the products:
\(E_{a,\text{rev(cat)}} = E_{\text{peak(cat)}} - E_{\text{products}}\)
\(E_{a,\text{rev(cat)}} = 90\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} - 20\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 70\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 4: Calculation of Enthalpy Change of the Reaction
The overall enthalpy change is determined strictly by the state function difference between products and reactants:
\(\Delta H = E_{\text{products}} - E_{\text{reactants}}\)
\(\Delta H = 20\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} - 50\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = -30\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
This value is identical for both the uncatalyzed and catalyzed pathways.

Step 5: Final Answer
The activation energy for the reverse catalyzed reaction is \(70\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and the reaction enthalpy change is \(-30\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: \(E_{a,\text{rev(cat)}} = 70\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta H = -30\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q05 - Activation energy and pre-exponential factor from Arrhenius plot

questiontext.text:
The linear plot of natural logarithm of the rate constant, \(\ln k\), versus the inverse of absolute temperature, \(1/T\) (in \(\text{K}^{-1}\)), for a gaseous thermal decomposition reaction is shown below:

Given the universal gas constant \(R = 8.314\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\), what are the activation energy (\(E_a\)) and the value of \(\ln A\) for this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Coordinates
The graph plots \(\ln k\) against \(1/T\) (with values scaled by \(10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}\)).
Two points on the straight line are:
Point 1: \((1/T)_1 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}\), \(\ln k_1 = -3.0\)
Point 2: \((1/T)_2 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}\), \(\ln k_2 = -13.0\)
Universal gas constant: \(R = 8.314\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
The logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation is:
\(\ln k = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A\)
Comparing this with the linear relation \(y = mx + c\):
\(\text{Slope } m = -\frac{E_a}{R}\)
\(\text{Intercept } c = \ln A\)

Step 3: Calculation of Slope and Activation Energy
The slope of the line is:
\(m = \frac{\ln k_2 - \ln k_1}{(1/T)_2 - (1/T)_1} = \frac{-13.0 - (-3.0)}{(3.0 - 2.0)\times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}} = \frac{-10.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}} = -10000\text{ K}\)
Since \(m = -E_a/R\):
\(E_a = -m \times R = -(-10000\text{ K}) \times 8.314\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 83140\text{ J}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 83.14\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 4: Calculation of \(\ln A\)
Substitute Point 1 into the Arrhenius equation:
\(\ln k_1 = m(1/T)_1 + \ln A\)
\(-3.0 = (-10000\text{ K})(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}) + \ln A\)
\(-3.0 = -20.0 + \ln A\)
\(\ln A = -3.0 + 20.0 = 17.0\)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with Point 2:
\(\ln k_2 = -10000 \times (3.0 \times 10^{-3}) + 17.0 = -30.0 + 17.0 = -13.0\), which is completely consistent.
The activation energy is \(83.14\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\ln A = 17.0\).
Final Answer: \(E_a = 83.14\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\ln A = 17.0\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICAL_KINETICS_MCQ_Q06 - Instantaneous and average rate evaluation from concentration time curve

questiontext.text:
The concentration of reactant \([\mathrm{R}]\) as a function of time \(t\) for a chemical reaction is plotted below. A tangent to the curve is constructed at \(t = 200\text{ s}\):

From the graphical data and the tangent line shown, calculate the average rate of reaction (\(r_{\text{av}}\)) over the time interval from \(100\text{ s}\) to \(300\text{ s}\), and the instantaneous rate of reaction (\(r_{\text{inst}}\)) at \(t = 200\text{ s}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the curve coordinates for the time interval from \(t_1 = 100\text{ s}\) to \(t_2 = 300\text{ s}\):
\([\mathrm{R}]_1 = 0.082\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\)
\([\mathrm{R}]_2 = 0.054\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\)
From the tangent line drawn at \(t = 200\text{ s}\), two distinct points on the tangent are:
\((t_a, [\mathrm{R}]_a) = (0\text{ s}, 0.092\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1})\)
\((t_b, [\mathrm{R}]_b) = (400\text{ s}, 0.040\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1})\)

Step 2: Formulae for Rates of Reaction
The average rate of disappearance of reactant \(\mathrm{R}\) over a time interval \(\Delta t = t_2 - t_1\) is given by:
\(r_{\text{av}} = -\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{R}]}{\Delta t} = -\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_2 - [\mathrm{R}]_1}{t_2 - t_1}\)
The instantaneous rate of reaction at time \(t\) equals the negative slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that time:
\(r_{\text{inst}} = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{R}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\text{Slope of tangent} = -\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_b - [\mathrm{R}]_a}{t_b - t_a}\)

Step 3: Calculation of Average Rate
Substitute the values for the interval from \(100\text{ s}\) to \(300\text{ s}\):
\(r_{\text{av}} = -\frac{0.054 - 0.082}{300 - 100}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} = -\frac{-0.028}{200}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} = 1.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)

Step 4: Calculation of Instantaneous Rate
Calculate the slope of the tangent line at \(t = 200\text{ s}\):
\(\text{Slope} = \frac{0.040 - 0.092}{400 - 0}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} = \frac{-0.052}{400}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} = -1.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)
Therefore:
\(r_{\text{inst}} = -(-1.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}) = 1.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)

Step 5: Final Answer
The average rate between \(100\text{ s}\) and \(300\text{ s}\) is \(1.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\) and the instantaneous rate at \(t = 200\text{ s}\) is \(1.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: \(r_{\text{av}} = 1.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\) and \(r_{\text{inst}} = 1.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)
